Enabling Test
Best Mode Test

rationale: Since the manufacturer's names (a distinguishing, dominant feature) are apparently different, but the overall label designs, colors, print styles, and sizes are similar, the appropriate test is the Holistic Test, which considers the entirety or the totality of the features of the trademarks/labels involved, rather than focusing on a single dominant feature (as under the Dominancy Test, which would look primarily at the most prominent/dominant feature of the mark, such as the differing brand name here, to assess likelihood of confusion).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: The Holistic Test for trademark infringement considers the entirety of the labels' features (design, color scheme, print style, size) rather than isolating a single dominant element, and is applied when the overall presentation, not just the brand name, creates the likelihood of confusion.

prompt: Which is false about contract of chattel mortgage?

choices.text: Registration of the chattel mortgage is made in the Chattel Mortgage Registry of the Register of Deeds where the property is located

Aside from the Chattel Mortgage Registry of the Register of Deeds where the property is located , registration shall also be made where the mortgagor resides if he resides in a place other than where the property is located
Where the parties executed a chattel mortgage on a building, they shall be bound to the chattel mortgage contract
Failure to execute the Affidavit of Good Faith and to register the chattel mortgage shall invalidate the mortgage.

rationale: Failure to execute the affidavit of good faith or to register a chattel mortgage does NOT invalidate the mortgage as BETWEEN the parties themselves (it remains a valid and binding contract between mortgagor and mortgagee); the absence of registration and/or the affidavit of good faith only affects its validity and enforceability as AGAINST third persons (such as other creditors or subsequent purchasers), making choice (d)'s blanket claim of invalidity the false statement.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A chattel mortgage's lack of registration or absence of an affidavit of good faith does not invalidate it as between the mortgagor and mortgagee; it only affects its binding effect as against third persons.

prompt: B purchased a residential lot of S for Php 1,000,000 on installment under the following terms: Php 200,000 downpayment on January 2, 2026; Php 100,000 every year thereafter until fully paid. Assumed that B defaulted on the very first installment due on January 2, 2027. What is the grace period to pay without additional interest and cash surrender value earned by B?

choices.text: 60 days and Php 0, respectively
60 days and Php 100,000, respectively
30 days and Php 100,000, respectively
No grace period and no cash surrender value

rationale: Under the Maceda Law (RA 6552), a buyer who has paid LESS THAN two (2) years of installments is entitled to a grace period of sixty (60) days from the date the installment became due, within which to pay without additional interest, but is NOT entitled to any cash surrender value (that refund right accrues only to buyers who have paid at least 2 years of installments). Since B, having paid only the initial downpayment before defaulting on the very first subsequent installment, has not yet completed 2 years of installment payments, B is entitled only to the 60-day grace period, with no cash surrender value.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Under the Maceda Law, a buyer who has paid less than two years of installments on a real estate installment sale is entitled only to a 60-day grace period to cure the default, without additional interest, but has no right to any cash surrender value.

prompt: Assume the same facts in preceding number, except that B defaulted on the installment due on January 2, 2033. What is the grace period to pay without additional interest and cash surrender value earned by B?

choices.text: 180 days and Php 440,000
210 days and Php 540,00
240 days and Php 620,000
150 days and Php 530,000

rationale: By the January 2, 2033 default, B has completed six full annual installment payments (2027 through 2032, P100,000 each = P600,000), plus the original P200,000 downpayment, for total payments of P800,000. Under the Maceda Law, the grace period is one month for every year of installment payments actually made (6 years of annual installments = 6 months = 180 days). The cash surrender value is 50% of total payments made, plus 5% for every year in excess of five years of installments paid (6 years - 5 = 1 additional year, so 50% + 5% = 55%); 55% x P800,000 = P440,000.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Under the Maceda Law, the grace period (one month per year of installments actually paid) and the cash surrender value (50% of total payments, plus 5% per year beyond five years) are computed based on the number of completed annual installment payments, exclusive of the initial downpayment.

prompt: Which of the following is not a characteristic of treasury share?

choices.text: It is an issued share but is not classified as outstanding share
It has no voting right
It may be sold at less than par value
It may be distributed as a stock dividend

rationale: Treasury shares CANNOT be distributed as stock dividends, since a stock dividend requires the issuance of new/unissued shares of the corporation representing a transfer of retained earnings to the capital account, whereas treasury shares are already-issued shares merely reacquired by the corporation and held in treasury — distributing them as a stock dividend would not represent a similar capitalization of retained earnings and is not the recognized mechanism for treasury share disposition (they are instead typically resold, retired, or otherwise disposed of at the board's discretion).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Treasury shares, being already-issued but non-outstanding shares held by the corporation, cannot be distributed as stock dividends, unlike newly-issued unissued shares.

prompt: Which of the following defects would make the corporate a de facto corporation

choices.text: The corporate name which resembles the name of a pre-existing corporation is likely to deceive the public but the certificate of registration has already been issued by SEC
Failure to file the articles of incorporation with the SEC
Absence of certificate of incorporation or registration from SEC
Continuing business operations despite the discovery of the defect or defects after incorporation without any action to correct them

rationale: A de facto corporation requires: (1) a valid law under which it could be incorporated, (2) a bona fide attempt to organize under that law, (3) actual user/exercise of corporate powers, and (4) issuance of a certificate of incorporation/registration by the SEC despite some defect in compliance with legal requirements (such as a deceptively similar corporate name). Since a certificate WAS actually issued in choice (a), this presents a genuine, curable defect in an otherwise good-faith attempt to incorporate — a hallmark of de facto corporate existence; choices (b) and (c), which involve the total absence of an SEC certificate, and choice (d), a continuing intentional non-correction of a known defect, do not qualify for de facto status.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A de facto corporation requires an actual SEC certificate of incorporation to have been issued despite some curable defect in the incorporation process, distinguishing it from cases where no certificate was ever issued at all.

prompt: Which is false about the board of directors of a stock corporation?

choices.text: A director must not have been convicted by a final judgment of an offense punishable by more than six (6) years of imprisonment, or committed a violation of the Corporation Code within five (5) years prior to the date of election or appointment

A director may be removed from office by a vote of the majority of the outstanding capital stock with or without cause; provided, that removal without cause may not be used to deprive minority stockholders, who used cumulative voting to elect such director, or the right of representation

No director shall receive any compensation (other than reasonable per diems) as such, unless the same is granted in the by-laws or but a vote of at least majority of the outstanding capital stock, provided, that the total yearly compensation (excluding reasonable per diems and compensation as officers) shall not exceed ten (10%) of the net income before tax of the corporation during the preceding year
Additional qualifications may be provided in the by-laws as long as they are reasonable and not contrary to law

rationale: Under Sec. 27 of the RCC, removal of a director requires a vote of stockholders holding or representing at least TWO-THIRDS (2/3), not merely a majority, of the outstanding capital stock — making choice (b)'s 'majority' figure the false/incorrect statement (the rest of choice b's content, on protecting minority representation elected through cumulative voting, is otherwise an accurate statement of the removal rule's proviso).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Removal of a corporate director, with or without cause, requires the vote of stockholders representing at least two-thirds of the outstanding capital stock, not merely a majority.

prompt: It refers to the restructuring of corporate capital where the outstanding shares are called in and replaced by a larger number, accompanied by a corresponding reduction in the par or stated value?

choices.text: Stock adjustment
Stock split up
Stock split down
Stock trading

rationale: A stock split-up (or 'stock split') is the process of converting each existing share into a greater number of shares with a proportionately reduced par or stated value per share, without changing the total capitalization or each stockholder's proportionate equity interest — as distinguished from a stock split-down (reverse split), which combines existing shares into a smaller number of shares with a correspondingly higher value each.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A stock split-up converts existing shares into a greater number of shares at a proportionately lower par or stated value each, without altering the corporation's total capitalization or each stockholder's proportionate interest.

prompt: X is a stockholder of ABC Corporation. He and other stockholders were recently denied of their pre-emptive right when the corporation increased its authorized capital stock and they were also prohibited to exercise the right to vote in the election of the board of directors. Which action may be filed by X against ABC Corporation

choices.text: Derivative suit for pre-emptive right and right to vote
Representative suit for pre-emptive right and right to vote
Representative suit for pre-emptive right and individual suit for right to vote
Individual suit for pre-emptive right and representative suit for right to vote

rationale: The pre-emptive right and the right to vote are both proprietary rights personal to each stockholder; since X's OWN pre-emptive right was individually violated, X may bring an INDIVIDUAL suit in his own behalf for that violation. However, since OTHER stockholders were similarly denied their right to vote (a common/shared injury affecting a class of stockholders), X may sue in a REPRESENTATIVE capacity, on behalf of himself and the other similarly affected stockholders, for the right-to-vote violation.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A stockholder may bring an individual suit for a violation of his own personal proprietary right (such as pre-emptive right), and a representative suit on behalf of himself and other similarly situated stockholders for a right violated in common (such as the right to vote).

prompt: Which is not an attribute of a close corporation?

choices.text: The officers or employees may be elected or appointed by the stockholders themselves rather than by the board of directors as may be provided in the article of incorporation
The pre-emptive right of stockholders does not extend to treasury shares
The holders of each class of stock may elect the allocated number of directors coming from their own class as provided in the articles of incorporation
Any amendment to the articles of incorporation must be approved by at least 2/3 of the outstanding capital stock with or without voting rights

rationale: In a CLOSE corporation specifically, the pre-emptive right of stockholders EXTENDS even to treasury shares and shares issued in exchange for property or in payment of a prior corporate debt — a notable expansion beyond the general rule for ordinary stock corporations (where pre-emptive rights do NOT extend to treasury shares); hence, choice (b), which asserts the general/ordinary rule as if applicable to close corporations, is the statement that does NOT correctly describe an attribute of a close corporation.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Unlike ordinary stock corporations, a close corporation's stockholders enjoy pre-emptive rights that extend even to treasury shares and shares issued for property or debt.

prompt: The following statements pertain to a voting trustee, except

choices.text: The representative acquires legal title to the shares
It is good only for the meeting for which it was intended
It is generally irrevocable and the representative may vote even in the presence of the stockholder
The agreement giving the representative the power to vote must be duly notarized and a copy thereof must be submitted to the SEC to be effective and enforceable

rationale: A voting TRUST agreement, unlike a mere proxy, transfers LEGAL TITLE to the shares to the voting trustee for the agreed period (generally up to 5 years, or coterminous with a loan agreement's life), making it valid for that entire period and not merely for a single meeting; choice (b)'s description (good only for the meeting intended) instead describes an ordinary PROXY, not a voting trust, making it the exception/incorrect statement among the choices.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A voting trust agreement transfers legal title to the shares to the trustee for its stated duration (unlike a mere proxy, which is limited to a specific meeting), and is generally irrevocable during that period.

prompt: The articles of incorporation of ABC Corporation provides for 7 directors. In the monthly meeting of the board of directors held on April 8, 2026, directors B, C, D and E were present and the following resolutions were approved: a. A resolution for the purchase of a delivery truck from E Trading, a sole proprietorship owned by E. B, C, D and E voted for the resolution. b. A resolution appointing T as the new corporate secretary where B, C, D and E voted for the resolution. Which is correct?

choices.text: Both resolutions are valid and do not need stockholders approval
Both resolutions are valid but need stockholders approval
Resolution a needs stockholders approval. Resolution b is valid
Resolution a is not valid. Resolution b needs stockholders approval

rationale: Resolution (a) involves a self-dealing director (E, through his sole proprietorship E Trading) whose presence (as one of only four directors present, out of 7) was necessary to constitute the quorum, and whose vote was likewise necessary for the resolution's approval — since these conditions for automatic validity under Sec. 31 of the RCC are not met, the contract is voidable at the corporation's option unless ratified by stockholders representing at least 2/3 of the outstanding capital stock with full disclosure. Resolution (b), appointing a new corporate secretary, is an ordinary matter squarely within the board's own competence and validly approved by the requisite board majority, requiring no stockholder approval.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A self-dealing director's contract approved when his presence or vote was necessary for board quorum/approval requires stockholder ratification (2/3 of outstanding capital stock), unlike the board's ordinary appointment of a corporate officer, which needs no stockholder approval.

prompt: A sells to B a Sony colored TV for P12,000 payable in twelve equal monthly installments beginning May 5, 2026 and every 5th day of each month thereafter. The contract provides that upon failure to pay any installment due, the whole balance becomes due and demandable. To secure the obligation, a chattel mortgage over the TV set was executed When B defaulted on the seventh and eighth installments, A sued B for the payment of the whole balance of P6,000. The TV set was levied and subsequently sold at a public sale for P5,000. Can A still recover the deficiency of P1,000 from B?

choices.text: Yes, if there was stipulation to that effect
Yes, even though there was no stipulation
No, any stipulation allowing recovery is void
No, if there was no stipulation to that effect

rationale: Wait, under Art. 1484(3) (Recto Law), when the vendor chooses to foreclose the chattel mortgage constituted on the thing sold for failure to pay two or more installments, he shall have NO FURTHER ACTION to recover any unpaid balance/deficiency — this is an absolute statutory bar that applies regardless of any stipulation purporting to allow deficiency recovery; any such stipulation to the contrary is void, so A cannot recover the P1,000 deficiency at all, whether or not there was a stipulation.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Under the Recto Law, a vendor who forecloses the chattel mortgage on personal property sold in installments after the buyer's default may not recover any deficiency, and any stipulation purporting to allow such recovery is void.

prompt: A person cannot be admitted into the partnership without the consent of

choices.text: All the partners
Majority of the partners
2/3 of the partners
Partners representing the controlling interest

rationale: Under Art. 1804 (in relation to the delectus personae principle underlying partnership law), no person can be admitted as a new partner into an existing partnership without the consent of ALL the existing partners, since a partnership is founded on the mutual trust and confidence of the partners in each other.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Admission of a new partner into an existing partnership requires the unanimous consent of all the existing partners, reflecting the personal trust and confidence (delectus personae) underlying the partnership relation.

prompt: A, B and C formed ABC & Co. a limited partnership with A as general partner, B as limited partner and C as industrial partner. A and B contributed P50,000 each. The partnership failed and after disposing all its assets to pay partnership debts, there still remains payable in the sum of P15,000 representing a down payment made by a customer which was pocketed by partner A. Against whom can the creditor demand payment of the P15,000

choices.text: Only A is liable to pay the P15,000 indebtedness
B is liable to pay P15,000
Only A or C is liable to pay P15,000
A, B and C are liable to pay P5,000 each

rationale: The down payment pocketed by A was money received by the partnership itself in the ordinary course of its business (a customer's down payment for a partnership transaction), making the resulting P15,000 obligation a genuine partnership debt rather than A's purely personal liability. Under Art. 1858, a limited partner is liable to partnership creditors to the extent of any part of his contribution wrongfully returned to him, or for the difference between his contribution actually made and that stated as made; here, with partnership assets already exhausted and A's own share unable to fully answer for this remaining obligation, B, as the limited partner whose capital contribution remains a fund answerable to partnership creditors, is called upon to satisfy this shortfall up to his P50,000 contribution — of which the P15,000 claim can be satisfied.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A limited partner's capital contribution remains a fund available to partnership creditors to the extent of his stated contribution, and may be called upon to satisfy a partnership obligation once partnership assets and the general partner's own resources prove insufficient.

prompt: When a real property is contributed to the partnership, which is correct?

choices.text: A real contract is perfected
A written instrument is required
A public instrument complete with inventory is required
A partner can make important alteration if beneficial to the partnership

rationale: Under Art. 1771 and 1773, when immovable property (or real rights) is contributed to a partnership, the contract must be in a PUBLIC INSTRUMENT, and an INVENTORY of the property contributed must be made, signed by the parties, and attached to the public instrument; otherwise, the partnership contract, insofar as it involves the contribution of immovables, is VOID.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A partnership contract involving the contribution of immovable property requires a public instrument with an attached, signed inventory of the property contributed, without which the contract of partnership is void.

prompt: In case the remaining members of the board of directors of a corporation still constitute a quorum, and there are vacancies, who will fill up such vacancies? Removal / Resignation / Expiration of term / Increase in the number of Directors / Death

choices.text: Stockholders / Board / Stockholders / Stockholders / Board
Stockholders / Board / Stockholders / Stockholders / Stockholders
Stockholders / Board / Stockholders / Stockholders / Stockholders
Stockholders / Board / Board / Stockholders / Board

rationale: Under Sec. 28 of the RCC, vacancies caused by REMOVAL, EXPIRATION OF TERM, or an INCREASE in the number of directors must always be filled by the STOCKHOLDERS; vacancies caused by RESIGNATION and DEATH, however, may be filled by the vote of the remaining directors constituting a quorum, since these are causes 'other than removal or expiration of term' contemplated by the statute.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Vacancies from removal, expiration of term, and an increase in the number of directors must be filled by the stockholders; vacancies from resignation or death may instead be filled by the remaining directors constituting a quorum.

prompt: A obtained a loan of Php 300,000 from B payable on March 25, 2022. As security for the payment of his loan, A constituted a mortgage on his residential house and lot in B's favor. C, a good friend of A, guaranteed and obligated himself to pay B in case A fails to pay his loan at maturity. If A fails to pay B his loan on March 25, 2022, can B compel C to pay?

choices.text: No. В cannot compel C to pay because as guarantor, C can invoke the principle of excussion, i.e., all assets of B must first be exhausted.
No. В cannot compel C to pay because B has not exhausted the available remedies against A
Yes. B can compel C to pay because the nature of C's undertaking indicates that he has bound himself solidarily with A
Yes. B can compel C who bound himself to unconditionally pay in case A fails to pay, thus the benefit of excussion will not apply.

rationale: C's undertaking, as described ('guaranteed and obligated himself to pay B in case A fails to pay'), is an ordinary GUARANTY (not suretyship), which is subsidiary in nature; under Art. 2058, the guarantor cannot be compelled to pay unless the creditor (B) has exhausted all the property of the DEBTOR (A) and resorted to all legal remedies against the principal debtor first (benefit of excussion).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: An ordinary guarantor may invoke the benefit of excussion, requiring the creditor to first exhaust all legal remedies against the principal debtor before proceeding against the guarantor.

prompt: If A sells his residential house and lot to D, can B foreclose the real estate mortgage?

choices.text: Yes. B can foreclose the real estate mortgage because real estate mortgage creates a real right that attaches to the property
Yes. B can foreclose the real estate mortgage, It is binding upon D as the mortgage is embodied in a public instrument
No, В cannot foreclose the real estate mortgage. The sale confers ownership on the buyer, D, who must therefore consent
No. В cannot foreclose the real estate mortgage. To deprive the new owner of ownership and possession is unjust and inequitable.

rationale: A real estate mortgage, to bind third persons such as a subsequent buyer D, must be embodied in a public instrument and duly registered (Art. 2125); once so recorded, the mortgage is binding upon and enforceable against D despite the subsequent sale, since D takes the property charged with notice of the recorded encumbrance. B may thus foreclose the mortgage against the property even after A's sale to D, precisely because the mortgage was constituted in a public instrument giving it binding effect against third persons who subsequently deal with the property.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A real estate mortgage embodied in a public instrument (and duly registered) binds subsequent buyers of the mortgaged property, allowing the mortgagee to foreclose despite an intervening sale to a third person.

prompt: Cruz lent Jose his car until Jose finish his Bar Examination. Soon after Cruz delivered the car, Jose brought it to Mitsubishi Cubao for maintenance check-up and incurred a cost of Php 8,000. Seeing the car's peeling and faded paint, Jose also had the car repainted for Php 10,000. After the Bar Exam, Cruz asked for the return of his car. Jose said he would return it as soon as Cruz has reimbursed him for the car maintenance and repainting cost of Php 18,000. Is Jose's refusal justified?

choices.text: No. Jose's refusal is not justified. In this kind of contract, Jose is obliged to pay for all the expenses incurred for the preservation of the thing loaned.
Yes. Jose's refusal is justified. He is obliged to pay for all the ordinary and extraordinary expenses, but subject to reimbursement from Cruz
Yes. Jose's refusal is justified. The principle of unjust enrichment warrants the reimbursement of Jose's expenses
No. Jose's refusal is not justified. The expenses he incurred are useful for the preservation of the thing loaned. It is Jose's obligation to shoulder these useful expenses.

rationale: This is a contract of commodatum; under Art. 1941, the bailee (Jose) is obliged to pay for the ORDINARY expenses for the use and preservation of the thing loaned (such as routine maintenance and repainting to preserve the car's condition), without a right to withhold return or demand reimbursement for these — only EXTRAORDINARY, unforeseen, and urgent expenses (which these routine maintenance/repainting costs are not shown to be) may be subject to a right of retention/reimbursement under Art. 1949; Jose's refusal to return the car pending reimbursement for these ordinary preservation expenses is thus not justified.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: In a commodatum, the bailee must shoulder the ordinary expenses for the use and preservation of the thing loaned without a right to withhold return pending reimbursement, unlike extraordinary, unforeseen, or urgent expenses which may entitle the bailee to reimbursement.

prompt: As lending investor, Gary granted a Php 1M loan to Isaac to be paid within two years from the execution of the contract. As security for the loan, Isaac promised to deliver to Gary his Toyota Innova within seven days but Isaac failed to do so. Gary was thus compelled to demand payment for the loan before the end of the agreed two year term. Can Gary compel Isaac to pay his loan even before the end of the two year period?

choices.text: Yes. Gary can compel Isaac to immediately pay the loan. Noncompliance with the promised guaranty or security renders the obligation immediately demandable. Isaac lost his right to make use of the period.

Yes. Gary can compel Isaac to immediately pay the loan. The delivery of the Toyota Innova is a condition for the loan. Isaac's failure to deliver the car violated the condition upon which the loan was granted. It is but fair for Gary to demand immediate payment.

No. Gary cannot compel Isaac to immediately pay the loan. The delivery of the car as security for the loan is an accessory contract, the principal contract is still the Php 1M loan. Thus, Isaac can still make use of the period

No. Gary cannot compel Isaac to immediately pay the loan. Equity dictates that Gary should have granted a reasonable extension of time for Isaac to deliver his Toyota Innova. It would be unfair and burdensome for Isaac to pay the Php 1M simply because the promised security was not delivered

rationale: Under Art. 1198(2), the debtor loses the right to make use of the period (making the obligation immediately demandable) when he fails to fulfill the guaranties or securities he has promised to the creditor; here, Isaac's failure to deliver the promised Toyota Innova security within the agreed 7 days constitutes exactly such non-compliance, entitling Gary to demand immediate payment of the loan even before the 2-year term expires.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Under Art. 1198, a debtor who fails to deliver the security/guaranty he promised to the creditor loses the benefit of the period and the obligation becomes immediately demandable.

prompt: Which of the following defense is meritorious?

choices.text: An action for recovery of down payment paid under a rescinded oral sale of real property
A defense in an action for ejectment that the lessor verbally promised to extend or renew the lease.
An action for payment of sum of money filed against one who orally promised to answer another's debt in case the latter defaults.
A defense in an action for damages that the debtor has sufficient, but unliquidated asset to satisfy the credit acquired when it becomes due.

rationale: The Statute of Frauds (Art. 1403) applies only to the enforcement of executory contracts still to be performed, not to actions for the recovery of what has already been paid or delivered under a contract that has been consummated, rescinded, or otherwise partially executed; an action for the recovery of a down payment under a rescinded (albeit oral) sale of real property is therefore not barred by the Statute of Frauds and constitutes a meritorious cause of action.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: The Statute of Frauds bars only the enforcement of still-executory unwritten contracts falling within its scope; it does not bar an action to recover payments already made under a contract that has since been rescinded or executed.

prompt: A, B, C and D are partners in AB and Company, contributing Php 20,000, Php 30,000, Php 50,000 and industry respectively. Due to financial reverses, they decided to dissolve the partnership. At the time of dissolution only Php 10,000 is left but the obligation to Y - Php 50,000; to partner B - Php 30,00 and to partner C - Php 20,000 remain unpaid. Which of the following is not correct if there is no profit and loss sharing agreement?

choices.text: The partnership, A, B, C and D will pay Y Php 10,000 each
Y can collect Php 10,000 each from partners A, B, C and D
D is exempt from loss, but not from liability to Y.
Y can collect P10,000 from the partnership, P8,000 from A, P12,000 from B and P20,000 from C

rationale: Under Art. 1839's priority rule, the remaining P10,000 partnership assets are applied first to the outside creditor Y, leaving a P40,000 deficiency chargeable against the general partners (A, B, C, D) for Y's benefit. As between the partners themselves, D, being an INDUSTRIAL partner, is exempt from bearing LOSSES internally (Art. 1797) but remains liable, along with the capitalist partners, to the OUTSIDE creditor Y on a pro rata (equal-share) basis (Art. 1816). Since choices (a) and (b) correctly reflect the equal P10,000-per-partner sharing of Y's deficiency (with D still liable to Y despite being exempt from internal loss-sharing), and choice (d) instead allocates the deficiency in unequal, capital-proportional amounts (excluding D and using figures inconsistent with the equal pro rata rule for outside-creditor liability), choice (d) is the incorrect statement.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: An industrial partner, though exempt from internally bearing partnership losses, remains liable pro rata (in equal shares) with the capitalist general partners to satisfy an outside creditor's unpaid claim after partnership assets are exhausted.

prompt: When a partner has been appointed manager in the articles of partnership, which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: He may execute all acts of administration despite the opposition of his partners unless he acts in bad faith
His power is irrevocable without just or lawful cause
If with just or lawful cause, his appointment can be revoked by majority vote of the partners
If without just or lawful cause, his appointment can be revoked only with the consent of all the partners including the managing partner

rationale: Under Art. 1800, a partner appointed manager in the articles of partnership (a condition of the partnership contract itself) may have his power revoked only for JUST OR LAWFUL CAUSE, and such revocation requires the VOTE OF THE PARTNERS REPRESENTING THE CONTROLLING INTEREST (not merely a numerical 'majority of the partners'), making choice (c)'s description of the required vote ('majority vote of the partners') the incorrect statement.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A managing partner appointed under the articles of partnership may be revoked for just cause only by the vote of partners representing the controlling interest, not merely a numerical majority of the partners.

prompt: If two or more partners have been entrusted with the management of the partnership without a stipulation that one of them shall not act without the consent of all the others or without specification of their respective duties. Which of the following is correct?

choices.text: Each one may separately execute all acts of administration despite the opposition of his partners
If any of the managing partners should oppose the act of the others, the decision of majority of all the partners shall prevail
In case any of the managing partners oppose the acts of the others, the matter shall be decided by the managing partners owning the controlling interest
In case of opposition by the other managing partners, the decision of the majority of the managing partners shall prevail

rationale: Under Art. 1801, where two or more managing partners are appointed without specification of duties and without a unanimity/veto stipulation, each may separately execute acts of administration, BUT in case of OPPOSITION by any of the other managing partners, the decision of the MAJORITY OF THE MANAGING PARTNERS themselves shall prevail; only in case of a TIE among the managing partners is the matter then referred to the partners owning the controlling interest.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: When two or more managing partners are appointed without specified duties, the majority of the managing partners themselves resolves any disagreement among them, with resort to the partners owning the controlling interest reserved for a tie vote among the managers.

prompt: A, B, C and D are partners in AB and Company. A parcel of land in the name of AB and Company was sold by A in the name of AB and Company but without express authority to Y, which of the following is correct?

choices.text: Title to the property passes to Y even if AB and Company is not engaged in buying and selling of land if Y acted in good faith
AB and Company may recover the land if it is not engaged in selling of land
If Y donated the land to W, AB and Company can no longer recoyer such land
AB and Company may recover the land from Y because the sale made by A to Y is unenforceable

rationale: Under Art. 1818, a conveyance of REAL property owned by the partnership, executed by a partner in the partnership name but WITHOUT authority to bind the partnership in that particular transaction (i.e., outside the usual course of the partnership's actual business, such as selling land when the partnership is not engaged in the business of buying/selling land), does not bind the partnership; the partnership may thus RECOVER the property from the buyer (Y), unless the property has subsequently been transferred to an innocent purchaser for value who had no notice of the partner's lack of authority.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A partner's unauthorized sale of partnership real property outside the partnership's usual line of business does not bind the partnership, which may recover the property from the buyer absent a subsequent transfer to an innocent purchaser for value.

prompt: M, a minor owns a specific ring valued at Php 100,000. G, the guardian of M, by means of fraud induced B a minor to buy the ring for Php 75,000, which B did so and G effected delivery to B. The contract is not in writing. Which is correct? The contract is

choices.text: Unenforceable because Mand B are both incapacitated to give consent
Rescissible because M suffered a lesion of ¼ of the value of the ring
Voidable but G cannot ask for annulment of the contract
Voidable but B can only ask for annulment within 4years from discovery of the fraud

rationale: The contract is voidable due to the fraud employed in inducing B, a minor, to buy the ring (vitiated consent under Art. 1338-1390); however, under Art. 1397, the person responsible for the fraud (here, G, who committed the deception, acting as M's guardian/representative) is barred from asking for the annulment of the contract he himself fraudulently procured, even though the contract is otherwise voidable at the instance of the innocent party (B).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A contract vitiated by fraud is voidable, but the party who committed or is responsible for the fraud is barred under Art. 1397 from himself seeking its annulment.

prompt: Which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: The obligation to give a determinate thing includes that of delivering all its accessions and accessories even though they may not have been mentioned
If a person obliged to do something fails to do it, the same shall be executed at his cost
When the obligation consists in not doing, and the obligor does what has been forbidden him, it shall be undone at his expense
In reciprocal obligations, from the moment one of the parties fulfills his obligation, delay by the other begins upon demand.

rationale: Under Art. 1169 (last paragraph), in reciprocal obligations, delay by the other party begins NOT upon demand, but from the moment ONE PARTY FULFILLS HIS OBLIGATION (i.e., the other party's obligation becomes immediately due and demandable, and delay is incurred automatically), without need for a separate demand — making choice (d)'s claim that demand is still required the incorrect statement. (Choices a, b, and c correctly restate Arts. 1166, 1167, and 1168, respectively.)

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: In reciprocal obligations, once one party performs his obligation, the other party is placed in default automatically, without need of a separate demand.

prompt: A, B and C solidarily owe W and Y, solidary creditors Php 24,000, where the share of the debtors is 2:3:5 while the creditors is 1:2. The terms of the contract provide: 1. A will pay if Y will pass the October 2026 CPA Board Exams; 2. B will pay on November 20, 2026; 3. C will pay on September 10, 2026. On September 10, 2026, W can collect from

choices.text: C = Php 8,000

rationale: The debtors' respective terms/conditions attach to their own INDIVIDUAL shares of the P24,000 debt (A:B:C = 2:3:5, i.e., A=P4,800, B=P7,200, C=P12,000). Only the debtor whose own term has actually arrived by September 10, 2026 has a matured, collectible share; A's share remains suspended pending an uncertain condition, so W's demand at this point is properly limited to the P12,000 aliquot share of the debtor whose term is presently due, rather than the full P24,000, since a solidary obligee cannot yet treat the still-unmatured shares of the other debtors as ripe for collection.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Where each solidary debtor's own aliquot share of an obligation is subject to a separate term or condition, the amount presently collectible by a solidary creditor is limited to whichever debtor's own share has actually matured, since the other debtors' shares are not yet ripe for collection.

prompt: Using the above data, the debtor who effected payment is entitled to get reimbursement from

choices.text: A or B = Php 12,000

rationale: After C pays the entire P24,000 to the solidary creditors, C is entitled to reimbursement from his co-debtors A and B, but ONLY for the shares of those co-debtors whose OWN obligations have ALREADY BECOME DEMANDABLE at the time of C's payment; since B's share becomes due only in November 2026 and A's share remains subject to a suspensive condition not yet fulfilled as of September 10, 2026, C cannot yet seek reimbursement from either A or B for their respective shares, since neither of their portions of the debt has become due as of the date of C's payment.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A solidary debtor who pays the entire obligation may seek reimbursement from co-debtors only to the extent their respective shares have themselves already become due and demandable at the time of payment.

prompt: On August 1, 2026, A agreed to give his only cow to B or to construct the house of B, if B will pass the October 2026 CPA Examination. The list of successful examinees was released on October 19, 2026 and B is one of those who passed the examination. As a result,

choices.text: A is entitled to the cow and the fruits if A decides to construct B's house
B is entitled to the cow and its fruits beginning October 19, 2026
B is entitled to the cow beginning August 1, 2026 and to its fruits beginning October 19, 2026
B can compel A to deliver the cow and the fruits or to require A to construct his house

rationale: This is an ALTERNATIVE obligation (to give the cow OR construct the house) subject to a SUSPENSIVE CONDITION (B passing the exam). Under Art. 1187, in obligations to give, the effects of the fulfillment of the condition retroact to the day of the CONSTITUTION of the obligation (August 1, 2026) — meaning B's right to the cow itself is deemed to have vested as of that date once the condition is later fulfilled. The SAME article, however, treats fruits and interests accruing DURING the pendency of the condition differently: absent contrary intent, these are not similarly backdated, and B becomes entitled to the fruits only from the date the condition was actually fulfilled (October 19, 2026) onward.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: In a conditional obligation to give, fulfillment of the suspensive condition retroacts the creditor's right to the thing itself back to the date the obligation was constituted, but entitlement to the fruits produced during the condition's pendency begins only from the date the condition was actually fulfilled.

prompt: A and B are solidary debtors of C for P100,000 which is due on August 1, 2027. Thinking that the obligation is already due, A paid C P100,000 on August 1, 2026. What rights will A have on February 1, 2027?

choices.text: A can recover P50,000 reimbursement from B without interest
A can recover P100,000 from C plus interest from August 1 2026 to February 1, 2027
A can recover P50,000 reimbursement from B with interest from August 1, 2026 to February 1, 2027
A cannot recover yet from either B because the obligation is not yet due or C because the payment was voluntary

rationale: Since the obligation was not yet due when A paid (a full year before the August 1, 2027 due date), A's payment to C was effectively a premature payment; A may recover this improperly-accepted premature payment from C, together with interest for the period the money was in C's hands ahead of its due date, since C is not entitled to retain an amount not yet actually owing to him. A cannot yet seek reimbursement from co-debtor B, however, since B's own share of the debt has itself not yet become due as of February 1, 2027.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A solidary debtor who mistakenly pays an obligation before it is actually due may recover the payment (with interest) from the creditor, but cannot yet seek reimbursement from a co-debtor until the debt itself becomes due.

prompt: Using the preceding number, but it is already September 1, 2027, which of the following is correct? A can recover

choices.text: A can recover from C only the interest from August 1, 2026 to July 31, 2027.
A can recover P50,000 from B plus interest from August 1, 2026 to August 1, 2027.
A can recover P50,000 from B plus interest from August 1, 2026 to September 1, 2027
A can recover from C only the interest from August 1, 2026 to September 1, 2027

rationale: Once the due date (August 1, 2027) has already arrived (it is now September 1, 2027, past maturity), A's premature payment made on August 1, 2026 is deemed to have effectively and validly extinguished the solidary obligation as of the due date, since C was already entitled to the principal amount once the obligation matured; A's recoverable claim against C is thus limited to the INTEREST for the period during which C held the funds before they were actually due (from August 1, 2026 until July 31, 2027, the day before the obligation matured).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Once the due date of a solidary obligation arrives after a co-debtor's premature payment, the paying debtor's recovery from the creditor is limited to interest for the period before maturity, since the principal payment is validly applied against the now-matured debt.

prompt: In a contract of sale, the parties agreed that the buyer shall be the one to fix the price subject to approval by the seller. The object was delivered to and accepted by the buyer. After a reasonable period of time, the buyer has not yet fixed the price but has appropriated the thing. The seller is now demanding for the payment of the price, in this case, the seller is

choices.text: Entitled to the payment of a reasonable price therefore.
Entitled to the payment of the price based on the fair market value at the time of delivery
Entitled to the payment of the price based on the fair market value at the time of perfection of the contract of sale
Not entitled to payment of the price because the price has not yet been fixed as agreed upon

rationale: Under Art. 1469, when the price is left to the fixing of one of the contracting parties, and that party fails to fix it within a reasonable time despite having appropriated or used the thing sold, the courts shall fix a REASONABLE PRICE therefor, since the buyer's appropriation of the thing without fixing the price cannot leave the seller without a remedy nor allow the buyer to unjustly enrich himself at the seller's expense.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Where a buyer tasked with fixing the price fails to do so within a reasonable time despite having already appropriated the thing sold, the seller is entitled to a reasonable price as determined by the courts.

prompt: Ting orally offered to sell his two hectare rice land to Gil for Php 10M. The offer was orally accepted. By agreement, the land was to be delivered (through execution of a notarized Deed of Sale) and the price was to be paid exactly one month from their oral agreement. Which statement is most accurate?

choices.text: If Ting refuses to deliver the land on the agreed date despite payment by Gil, the latter may not successfully sue Ting because contract is oral.
If Ting refused to deliver the land, Gil may successfully sue for fulfillment of the obligation even if he has not lendered payment of the purchase price
The contract between the parties is rescissible
The contract between the parties is subject to ratification by the parties

rationale: The oral sale of real property, being covered by the Statute of Frauds (Art. 1403[2][e]), is unenforceable by action unless ratified — such ratification may occur through partial performance, such as Gil's actual tender/payment of the purchase price and Ting's acceptance thereof, or through execution of the contemplated notarized Deed of Sale as the parties had agreed. Until such ratification occurs (e.g., through Gil's actual payment), the oral contract remains merely unenforceable, i.e., subject to ratification by the parties' subsequent acts.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: An oral sale of real property is unenforceable under the Statute of Frauds unless and until ratified by the parties, such as through partial performance (e.g., actual payment and acceptance) or execution of the contemplated written instrument.

prompt: Which phase most accurately completes the statement - If at the time the contract of sale is perfected, the thing which is the object of the contract has been entirely lost

choices.text: The buyer bears the risk of loss
The contract shall be without any effect
The seller bears the risk of loss
The buyer may withdraw from the contract

rationale: Under Art. 1493, if at the time the contract of sale is perfected, the thing which is the object of the sale has been entirely lost, the contract shall be WITHOUT ANY EFFECT (void/inexistent), since there is no object for the sale to operate upon — this reflects the principle that a thing already lost prior to or at perfection cannot be the object of a valid contract of sale.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: If the object of a sale has already been entirely lost at the time the contract is perfected, the contract of sale is without any effect, since it lacks an actual object.

prompt: A has two creditors, B and C, the obligation to B is PHP 10,000 and to C is PHP 12,000. Later, with the consent of A and B, W pays B PHP 10,000. Now W and C are the creditors of A. Suppose A has only PHP 12,000, which is correct?

choices.text: C should be preferred
W should be preferred
C and W should be paid proportionately
A may choose whom to pay

rationale: Since W paid B's credit with the consent of both A (the debtor) and B (the original creditor), W is legally SUBROGATED to B's rights as a creditor of A (Art. 1302[2], legal subrogation presumed when a third person, with the debtor's approval, pays another creditor); W thereby steps into B's shoes as an ordinary (unpreferred) creditor for P10,000, on equal footing with C's separate P12,000 claim — absent any special preference in favor of either credit, and A having insufficient funds (only P12,000) to satisfy both claims in full (totaling P22,000), the available amount should be distributed PROPORTIONATELY between W and C according to the amount of their respective credits.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A third party who pays a creditor with the consent of both debtor and that creditor is legally subrogated to the paid creditor's rights, and where the debtor's remaining funds are insufficient to satisfy all resulting ordinary credits in full, they should be shared proportionately among the creditors.

prompt: Which of the following is a valid stipulation?

choices.text: A promises to give B PHP 10,000, and if A fails, A will allow B to have sexual intercourse with her for one week
A will give B PHP 10,000, if C will go to planet Saturn within the year
A agreed to give B a house and lot if B will kill A's wife
A agreed to put poison on the food of B's wife and if A fails, to pay B PHP 10,000 for damages

rationale: This is a FACULTATIVE obligation: the PRINCIPAL prestation (A's promise to pay B P10,000) is entirely valid and lawful on its own; the immoral substitute prestation (allowing sexual intercourse in lieu of payment) is merely an ACCESSORY alternative the debtor may optionally resort to. Under the rules on facultative obligations, the invalidity of the substitute does not affect the validity of the principal obligation — since only one thing (the P10,000) is actually and primarily due, the stipulation as a whole remains a valid obligation to pay P10,000, with the void immoral clause simply unenforceable and severable. This differs from choices (c) and (d), where the entire prestation is itself conditioned on or constitutes an illegal act with no independently valid principal obligation to fall back on, rendering those stipulations void in their entirety.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: In a facultative obligation, where only one principal prestation is actually due and an accessory substitute is merely optional, the invalidity of an immoral or illegal substitute does not void the underlying valid principal obligation, which remains enforceable on its own.

prompt: A was having his house repaired by B, who needed construction materials, so A orally told the seller C, "Give B the materials, I shall be responsible. I shall pay in 30 days." C delivered the materials. As a result, the contract

choices.text: Is unenforceable because A made an oral agreement to answer for the debt of B
Is enforceable because A did not make a special promise to answer for the default of another person
Shall be enforceable if there is ratification by A
The contract shall be unenforceable if the value is at least PHP 500

rationale: The Statute of Frauds' requirement of a note or memorandum for 'a special promise to answer for the debt, default, or miscarriage of another' applies only to a COLLATERAL/secondary undertaking (a true guaranty of another's debt); here, A's statement ('Give B the materials, I shall be responsible, I shall pay in 30 days') constitutes an ORIGINAL, primary, direct undertaking by A himself to pay for the materials as his OWN obligation (not merely a promise to answer for B's debt if B defaults), so the Statute of Frauds provision on guaranties does not apply, and the oral agreement is fully enforceable.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: The Statute of Frauds' requirement for a written note applies only to a collateral promise to answer for another's debt, not to an original, primary undertaking by a person to pay for goods or services as his own direct obligation.

prompt: The liability of judgment debtor A under an obligation imposed by a final judgment is to pay PHP 10,000 but A and the judgment creditor B subsequently entered into a contract reducing the liability of A to only PHP 8,000. Which of the following is correct?

choices.text: There is an implied novation because the existing obligation is extinguished
Novation result in the extinguishment of an existing obligation and new one is substituted in its place
The payment by C of the reduced amount was the result of the new obligation
The agreement to reduce the judgment debt to PHP 8,000 completely extinguished the judgment debt and released A from his pecuniary liability

rationale: The subsequent agreement between A and B modifying/reducing the amount of the judgment debt constitutes a NOVATION by change of one of the principal conditions of the obligation (the amount owed), and novation, as a mode of extinguishing obligations, operates precisely by extinguishing the original obligation (here, the P10,000 judgment debt) and substituting a new one (the reduced P8,000 obligation) in its place — this general principle of novation (choice b) accurately describes the legal effect, whereas choices (a), (c), and (d) either mischaracterize this as an implied (rather than express) novation, refer to a non-existent third party (C), or overstate the effect as a complete release rather than a substitution of a new (reduced) obligation.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Novation, whether total or partial (such as merely reducing the amount owed), operates by extinguishing the original obligation and substituting a new obligation with modified terms in its place.

prompt: In order that consignation shall produce the effect of payment it is not only essential that it must conform with all the requisites of payment, but it is also essential that certain special requirements prescribed by law must be complied with. Which of the following is not correct?

choices.text: There must be a previous tender of payment
There is a debt due
The thing or amount due had been placed at the disposal of judicial authority
The notice previous to and after the consignation has been given to the persons interested in the fulfillment of the obligation

rationale: While a prior tender of payment is generally required before resorting to consignation, this is NOT an absolute/universal requirement — Art. 1256 expressly recognizes exceptions where consignation ALONE, WITHOUT need of a prior tender of payment, produces the effects of payment, such as when the creditor is absent or unknown, incapacitated to receive payment, or when two or more persons claim the right to collect, among other enumerated instances; hence choice (a)'s blanket assertion that prior tender is always essential is the INCORRECT statement.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Consignation generally requires a prior tender of payment, except in specific instances recognized under Art. 1256 (such as an absent, unknown, or incapacitated creditor) where consignation alone, without prior tender, produces the effect of payment.

prompt: A promissory note reads "I promise to pay B PHP 100,000 on May 10 2026. Sgd. A." B transferred the note to C. Later, X stole the promissory note and transferred the note to Y who received the note in good faith. On maturity date, Y presented the note to A and demanded payment. A paid the note in good faith. In this case

choices.text: C can recover from A
C can recover from B
A's obligation is extinguished
C can recover only from either X or Y

rationale: The note as worded ('I promise to pay B PHP 100,000...') is payable to a specifically named person without the words 'or order' or 'bearer,' making it a NON-NEGOTIABLE instrument. A non-negotiable instrument may still be transferred by ordinary civil-law assignment, but the transferee acquires no better title than the transferor had; since X, a thief, had no title at all to convey, Y (despite receiving the note in good faith) likewise acquired no valid title from X. Payment by A to Y — someone without valid title to the instrument — does not validly discharge A's obligation to C, the rightful holder who had validly received the note from B before the theft; C, having been deprived of payment through no fault of his own, may recover the amount from A.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: A promissory note payable to a specifically named person, without 'or order' or 'bearer' language, is non-negotiable; a thief conveys no valid title even to a good-faith transferee, so the maker's payment to that transferee does not discharge the maker's obligation to the rightful prior holder.

prompt: As a rule, when a creditor assigns his credit in good faith A) He warrants the collectability of the credit B) He warrants the existence of the credit at the time of assignment C) He warrants the legality of the credit at the time of assignment D) He warrants the solvency of the debtor at the time of assignment

choices.text: Only A and D
Only A and B
Only B and C
A, B, and C

rationale: Under Art. 1628, a person who assigns/sells a credit in good faith warrants the EXISTENCE of the credit and its LEGALITY at the time of the sale/assignment, but does NOT warrant the SOLVENCY of the debtor, nor the actual COLLECTABILITY of the credit, unless expressly stipulated or the assignor acted in bad faith.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: An assignor of credit who acts in good faith warrants only the existence and legality of the credit at the time of assignment, not the debtor's solvency or the credit's actual collectability, absent an express stipulation.

prompt: A granted a loan to B amounting to PHP 660,000 with 6% interest per annum. Such agreement was not reduced in writing but B paid the obligation and interest in cash and checks when A demanded payment. Which the following is correct?

choices.text: The payment of loan and interest is valid
The payment of loan and interest is void
B can demand the return of the amount representing the interest paid
The principle of solutio indebiti is applicable, hence B can recover the amount paid to A

rationale: Under Art. 1956, no interest shall be due on a loan unless it has been expressly stipulated IN WRITING; since the interest stipulation here was not reduced to writing (even though the principal loan itself is valid regardless of form), the interest portion of the agreement is legally void/unenforceable, entitling B, who nonetheless paid the interest, to demand its return (since it was not a debt legally due, notwithstanding that the principal loan repayment itself remains valid).

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: Under Art. 1956, interest on a loan is not legally due unless expressly stipulated in writing; interest paid pursuant to an unwritten stipulation may be recovered by the borrower even though the principal loan repayment itself remains valid.

prompt: Which of the following statements is not correct?

choices.text: If A gives his ring to B but it is not clear whether A donated it or merely lent it, the contract should be interpreted as commodatum rather than a donation
If A sells his car to B but A has four cars and it cannot be determined which car was sold, the contract of sale is void
A borrowed PHP 100,000 from B which bears interest at 12% per year but there is doubt whether it is payable in two or three years, the period of payment shall be interpreted at 2 years

A engaged the services of B but the contract did not indicate the amount of compensation to be paid, the amount thereof shall be the rate that is customarily paid in the place where the services were rendered

rationale: Under Art. 1378, when doubt arises as to the interpretation of a contract's terms and the contract is ONEROUS, doubts should be resolved in favor of the GREATEST RECIPROCITY OF INTERESTS between the parties; where there is doubt as to whether the loan period is 2 or 3 years, the greatest reciprocity of interests rule would favor interpreting the LONGER period (3 years, giving the debtor more time while the creditor continues earning interest), not automatically the shorter period, making choice (c)'s claim that the period should be interpreted as the SHORTER 2-year term the incorrect statement.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: In an onerous contract, doubt as to the interpretation of ambiguous terms (such as an uncertain loan period) is resolved in favor of the greatest reciprocity of interests between the parties, which generally favors the debtor being allowed the longer period.

prompt: In 2026, A promise to give to B his land if B passes the CPA board examination in 2027. If the condition is fulfilled, does A give the fruits for the period of 1 year?

choices.text: Yes, in obligation to give, once the condition is fulfilled the obligation shall retroact to the day of the constitution of the obligation
Yes, the creditor shall appropriate the fruits and interest, unless there is contrary intent
No, if the obligation is unilateral, the debtor shall appropriate the fruits and interest unless there is contrary intent
A and B will divide the fruits equally

rationale: Under Art. 1187, in obligations to give (as here), while the effects of the fulfilled condition generally retroact to the constitution of the obligation, the SAME article expressly provides that, with respect to fruits and interests DURING the pendency of the condition, the general rule is that these are deemed MUTUALLY COMPENSATED if the obligation is reciprocal (bilateral); but where the obligation is purely UNILATERAL (as a gratuitous promise, here A's promise to give land with no reciprocal counter-obligation from B), the DEBTOR (A) shall appropriate the fruits and interests accruing during the pendency of the condition, UNLESS a contrary intention appears from the nature or circumstances of the obligation.

source.center: CPA Review School of the Philippines (CPAR)

canonicalConcept: In a purely unilateral (gratuitous) conditional obligation to give, the debtor retains the fruits and interests accruing during the pendency of the condition, unless a contrary intention appears, distinguishing it from reciprocal obligations where such fruits are treated as mutually compensated.
